title: Fading View

patient.name: Mdm Ng Boon Huat
patient.presenting_complaint: Gradually worsening vision in both eyes over the past 2 years, worse in bright sunlight

history.hpc: Mdm Ng has noticed her vision has been getting progressively blurry over the past 2 years. She finds it particularly difficult to read small print and to thread her needle for sewing. She describes glare and dazzle when driving at night — oncoming headlights are especially bothersome, and she has stopped driving at night. Her vision is worse in bright sunlight. She denies any pain, redness, floaters, or flashing lights. She has been using steroid inhalers for asthma for the past 15 years.
history.pmhx: Asthma (on inhaled corticosteroids), no diabetes, no hypertension
history.social_hx: Lives with husband, formerly enjoyed sewing and reading, drives short distances during daytime only

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right: posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) — dense opacity at posterior pole of lens. Left: PSC with mild nuclear sclerosis. No corneal pathology bilaterally.

fundus.right: Difficult to visualise through dense PSC — red reflex reduced. Partial view: normal-looking disc and macula.
fundus.left: Reduced red reflex. Partial view showing normal disc, no obvious macular pathology.

refraction.right: Best corrected VA 6/12 — no improvement with further refraction (optical, not refractive cause)

investigations.oct_macula: Right: normal foveal contour, no pathology identified. Left: normal.
investigations.biometry: AL-scan performed for IOL power calculation in preparation for surgery

diagnosis: Bilateral posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC), left worse than right, likely steroid-induced from long-term inhaled corticosteroid use.

immediate: Explain diagnosis and natural history — cataracts are progressive, surgery is the only cure
Offer cataract surgery (phacoemulsification + intraocular lens implant) starting with the worse eye (left)
Discuss IOL options: monofocal (standard, glasses needed for reading), multifocal (spectacle independence), toric (if astigmatism present)
Pre-operative workup: biometry for IOL power, blood tests, anaesthetic assessment
Discuss risk minimisation of inhaled steroids with respiratory physician if possible
follow_up: Surgery on left eye first under local anaesthesia (peribulbar or topical)
Review at 1 day, 1 week, and 6 weeks post-op for vision and IOP
Plan right eye surgery once left eye has recovered (usually 4–6 weeks)
Refraction at 6 weeks post-op for final glasses prescription if using monofocal IOL
patient_education: Cataract surgery is one of the most commonly performed and safest surgeries in the world
Steroid inhalers can cause PSC — discuss with GP/respiratory physician about alternatives, but do not stop inhalers without advice
After surgery: avoid rubbing eyes, no swimming for 4 weeks, use prescribed eye drops
Posterior capsule opacification (PCO) can occur months to years later — treatable with a simple laser procedure (Nd:YAG)

key_points: Characterises visual symptoms: glare, dazzle, worse in bright light — classic PSC symptoms
Asks about steroid use (inhaled, topical, or systemic) — major cause of PSC
Asks about functional impact: driving, reading, daily activities
Excludes other causes: floaters, field loss, pain, redness
Checks pinhole VA to confirm optical (not refractive) cause
Slit lamp examination to characterise opacity type and density
Biometry for IOL power calculation prior to surgery
Links PSC to long-term steroid use
Offers phacoemulsification + IOL as definitive treatment
Steroid dose review with prescribing physician
